chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, from Abu Usamah, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the one in a state of major ritual impurity (junub) who sweats in his garment, or who bathes and then embraces his wife and lies with her while she is menstruating or in a state of major impurity, so that his body is affected by her sweat. He (peace be upon him) said: 'All of this is not [a problem].'.

key_terms.الْجُنُبِ: One in a state of major ritual impurity requiring ghusl
key_terms.لَيْسَ بِشَيْ‏ءٍ: It is nothing / not a problem (i.e., not impure)

ai.seo_question: Does the sweat of a person in major impurity (junub) or a menstruating woman make their clothes or body impure?
ai.summary: Reported by Ibn Udhaynah from Imam al-Sadiq (AS), this hadith establishes the principle that sweat from a person in major impurity (junub) or menstruation is not considered najis (impure), thereby resolving practical concerns regarding physical intimacy and clothing purity. This ruling is significant in Shia jurisprudence as it distinguishes between the ritual state of impurity (hadath) and physical impurity (najasah), allowing for normal bodily contact without requiring washing of the skin or garments. The Imam’s concise declaration 'this is nothing' underscores the ease and flexibility in daily worship and marital relations within the Shia legal tradition.
